chunks: "GP stands for general-purpose, meaning the pin isn't tied to one specific function.
A power pin always has to be power, a crystal pin always connects to the oscillator, and the reset pin is always reset.
A general-purpose pin has no assigned job until the software gives it one. I can choose whether it's an input or an output, drive it high or low, read it, or put a pull-up on it.
The nuance is that these pins are usually shared.
The same physical pin can be a plain GPIO, or it can be handed over to a peripheral, like UART TX, an SPI clock, a timer's PWM output or an ADC input.
That's called pin multiplexing or alternate functions, and a mux in front of the pad chooses which internal block is connected. And 'general' doesn't mean 'identical'.

In the datasheet some pins are 5 volt tolerant and some aren't, some can be analog inputs, some can wake the chip from sleep, some have higher drive strength, and a few are boot-mode straps that need a particular level at reset.
So when I plan a board I make a pin table and check each assignment against what that specific pin can do."
